paragraphs.text: "It’s springtime!" shouted Mole.
"Smell that fresh air!
But my house is so dusty and dirty," he said.
"I need a bucket. I need a mop. It’s time to clean!"
He stood on a ladder to dust a bookcase.
He moved a chair to clean under it.
He even polished the doorknobs!
"The kitchen is spotless!
The pots and pans are all washed.
The floor is next," said Mole.
Back and forth Mole scrubbed the floor.
"Ow!" he groaned. "My back is sore.
My arms are sore too."
Mole threw the scrub brush down.
"Forget it!" he said.
Mole grabbed his blue coat.
He ran up a tunnel to the outside.
"Up we go! Up we go!"
Mole’s head popped out of his hole.
"Wow, the sun is bright!"
Mole jumped out. "The grass smells sweet," he said.
He rolled in the grass.
He chased the butterflies.
"This is so much better than cleaning!" said Mole.
He ran across the meadow.
"Stop!" yelled an old rabbit.
"You must pay six pennies to run through here!"
Mole ran past the rabbit.
The old rabbit fell over.
The other rabbits came out of their holes.
They grumbled at the old rabbit.
"You should have yelled louder!" a gray rabbit said.
"You should have been bold!" said a small one.
"You should have told him the rules,"said a rabbit with a red ribbon.
But Mole didn't care.
"What a fine day for running!" said Mole.
Suddenly he stopped.
"What’s this?" asked Mole.
He saw something new.
A river! He sat on the riverbank.
"The water is so blue!" said Mole.
"How the waves sparkle!"
Mole looked across the water.
There was a hole in the other riverbank.
"What a cozy place to live!" Mole said.
A small face popped out of the hole.
It was the Water Rat.
"Hello, Mole!" said Water Rat, waving his hand.
"Hello, Rat!" said Mole.
"Would you like to come over?" asked Rat.
"Of course," said Mole happily.
Rat stepped into a little boat by his hole.
He rowed over to Mole.
"Step in!" said Rat.
"This is my first time in a boat!" cried Mole.
Rat was surprised. "What? Well!
Nothing is as great as being in a boat!"
Rat’s boat was beautiful, and it was blue.
Mole sat down on a cushion.
Rat began to row.
"This is so nice," said Mole.
"Yes, it’s perfect for two!" said Rat.
"It doesn’t matter where we go."
"It doesn’t?" asked Mole.
"No, what’s important is to enjoy the ride!" said Rat.
"Are we too near the riverbank?" Mole asked.
The muddy bank was getting closer.
Rat didn’t seem worried.
He was humming and rowing.
The bank was very close now.
Scared, Mole looked from side to side.
"Look out, Rat!" yelled Mole.
"We’re going to crash!"
The boat hit the bank and Rat flipped in the air.
Rat landed on his back.
"Oh, Rat, are you okay?" asked Mole.
"Of course!" said Rat, smiling.
"I’m so happy you’re fine," said Mole.
"Why don’t we row down the river?" asked Rat.
"We can spend the day together!"
"All right," Mole agreed.
"Oh, wait a moment," said Rat.
He brought out a basket from under a blanket.
Surprised, Mole asked, "What’s inside?"
"Cold chicken for lunch," said Rat.
"Rat, you have everything in your boat," cried Mole.
"And I am so hungry!"
Mole was happier than ever.
Rat rowed and Mole watched the waves.
Rat pointed to a rock near the bank.
"Look!" said Rat.
"That is where I caught my first fish."
But Mole didn’t hear him.
He was too busy enjoying the river.
"This is all new to me!" grinned Mole.
"The river is my world," said Rat.
"I don’t want any other."
"But it must be boring sometimes," said Mole.
"Never!" said Rat.
The river passed by some dark woods.
"What’s over there?" asked Mole.
"That? It’s the Wild Wood," said Rat.
"We Riverbankers don’t go there much."
"Are folks nice there?" asked Mole.
"The squirrels are all right.
Some of the rabbits are nice too.
But you can’t trust the weasels!" said Rat.
"Badger lives in the Wild Wood. He’s my friend."
"Let’s go see Badger!" Mole cried.
"That’s not a good idea," said Rat.
"Badger hates visitors."
Rat and Mole paddled into a small pond.
They tied up the boat and stepped out.
Rat spread the blanket. He opened the basket.
"Let’s eat!" cried Rat.
As they sat down, bubbles popped up on the water.
The bubbles moved closer to shore.
Splash ! A new friend popped out of the water.
"Hey! Why wasn’t I invited?" laughed Otter.
Rat was glad to see Otter.
Otter was a Riverbanker.
"Otter, this is Mole," said Rat.
"We’re just about to eat."
Sounds came from the bushes.
They all looked.
It was Badger!
He pushed through the leaves.
Badger stared at them. "Hmmph!" he said.
Badger turned and went into the bushes again.
"He didn’t say hello," said Mole, surprised.
"I told you," Rat said. "Badger likes to be alone."
After lunch Rat packed up the basket.
"Guess who is on the river today?" said Otter.
"Who?" asked Rat.
"Toad! He’s in his new racing boat," said Otter.
"Toad is always trying new things," said Rat.
"But he’s never good at them," laughed Otter.
"Well, I’m leaving!
Nice meeting you, Mole."
Mole was putting the oars in the boat.
"We're going too," said Rat.
"Oh, Rat, please let me row," cried Mole.
"Not yet. You need a few lessons," said Rat.
Mole climbed into the boat.
Rat hopped in and untied the boat.
"Rowing can’t be very hard," Mole thought.
Quickly he grabbed the oars!
"Stop, you’ll make us tip over!" cried Rat.
The boat tipped back and forth.
Mole lost his balance.
Sploosh ! They fell into the cold water.
The water was cold. Mole could not swim!
"How stupid of me!" Mole thought.
He started to sink.
Just in time, a paw grabbed Mole’s fur.
Whoosh ! Mole’s head popped above the waves.
"Oh!" gasped Mole.
"I’ve got you," said Rat. "You’ll be all right."
He pulled Mole to shore.
"Rat, I am very sorry," said Mole.
"Don’t worry about it," laughed Rat.
"What’s a little water to a Water Rat?"
He pulled the boat to shore.
They stepped into the boat again.
This time Mole sat quietly on his cushion.
Rat took the oars and rowed.
"We’ll be home soon," said Rat.
Rat’s home was a very cozy place.
Its shelves were full of books.
"Sit down and warm up," said Rat.
"I will light a bright fire."
"Ah-choo!" Mole sneezed.
"Here are slippers and a robe," said Rat.
"Put them on, Mole."
Together they ate a fine supper.
Then Rat sat with Mole by the fire.
Rat loved to write songs and poems.
He told Mole many stories of the river.
"You should stay with me," said Rat.
"I’ll teach you to row and swim."
"Thank you, Ratty," said Mole.
"You are a good friend!"
Rat and Mole waved at ducks from the riverbank.
"Rowing and swimming are great fun," Mole said.
Mole felt like an expert now.
"Here is a poem for the ducks!" said Rat.
Ducks can swim on the river,
Ducks can swim on the sea,
Ducks can swim most anywhere,
But not in an apple tree.
"I don’t like your poem much," said Mole, smiling.
The ducks stuck their heads under the water.
"The ducks don’t either!" laughed Rat.
"I was wondering," said Mole.
"Could I meet Toad?"
"What a great idea!" Rat said.
"We’ll paddle right there!"
Mole untied the boat.
Rat rowed them down the river.
"Toad must be very nice," said Mole.
"He is very friendly," said Rat. "But not too clever."
"Not everybody is clever," said Mole.
"Yes," agreed Rat. "But Toad, well . . .
he thinks he is more clever than he is."
The river curved as they rowed along.
Suddenly a grand house came into sight.
"There’s Toad Hall!" said Rat.
Rat rowed the boat to shore.
They climbed out and walked to the house.
Many boats were piled up on the grass.
"Oh no," Rat said. "Toad is finished with boating.
I wonder what he is up to now."
Toad was sitting by his boats.
He looked up from a map. "Hooray!" cried Toad.
He danced around Mole and Rat.
"What are you up to now, Toad?" asked Rat.
"How wonderful!" cried Toad.
"Friends to travel with!"
Rat looked a little worried.
"You have a nice home," said Mole shyly.
"Finest house on the whole river!" said Toad.
"In the whole world! "
Rat winked at Mole.
"Toad is always saying that," said Rat.
Toad giggled. "Oh, Ratty," he said.
"That’s just the way I am."
Rat pointed to the pile of boats.
"How is your boating going?"
"Boating?" cried Toad.
"Forget that! It’s a waste of time!"
"What?" Rat said.
"Come with me, Rat. Bring your friend!" said Toad.
They all walked to the stable.
"There you are!" Toad pointed to a new yellow cart.
"The open road! Travel and adventure!" cried Toad.
"Harrumph!" Rat put his hands in his pockets.
Mole stepped into the cart to look.
His eyes opened wide with wonder.
"I’ve got everything inside," said Toad.
"Beds, a stove, pots and pans!
All the food you can eat!"
"There’s even a bird in a cage!" said Mole.
"We start our trip this afternoon!" shouted Toad.
Toad hopped around his new yellow cart.
"Toad seems very excited," said Mole.
"Did he say we are going on a trip?" asked Rat.
Toad stopped in front of them.
"Well, I can’t go all by myself!" said Toad.
"Forget it!" said Rat.
"But you must see the world!" cried Toad.
"My world is the river," said Rat.
"Well, a trip might be fun," said Mole.
Rat frowned and crossed his arms.
"We don’t have to decide now," said Toad.
"Lunch is ready!"
They all went into the house.
They sat down at the dining table.
Everything inside was nice and fancy.
The food was excellent.
"There is nothing like traveling by cart!" said Toad.
Toad spread his map across the table.
He pointed at places they could visit.
"Every day you see something new!" Toad said.
"It sounds so exciting!" said Mole.
Rat looked up from his plate.
"Do you really want to go?" he asked Mole.
Mole nodded eagerly.
"Well, okay," said Rat.
"Hooray!" said Toad.
They went out to the stable again.
Toad tied his gray horse up to the cart.
Mole and Rat climbed in.
Toad took the reins. "Off we go!" cried Toad.
Toad, Mole, and Rat rode in the cart.
They were tired and covered in dust.
The sun was setting.
The sky was pink with the fading light.
"Let’s stop for the night," said Rat.
"Yes, let’s," said Mole.
"Wonderful idea!" said Toad. "I’m hungry."
They stopped the cart and untied the horse.
The stars came out in the dark sky.
They ate a simple supper under the moon.
"Time for bed," said Toad.
He snuggled under his blanket on the grass.
"What a great day!" he said.
"So much better than that old river."
Toad closed his eyes and began to snore.
"Oh, my river," sighed Rat. "I miss it very much."
Mole lay next to Rat.
He squeezed Rat’s paw.
"Rat," said Mole, "should we run away tomorrow?
We can go home to the river."
"No," said Rat. "We have to stay with Toad.
It would not be safe to leave him."
Mole yawned. "Okay."
"Toad’s foolish ideas never last long," said Rat.
Rat was right. Tomorrow everything would change.
"Goodnight, Mole," yawned Rat.
But Mole was already fast asleep.
The stars faded and the sun rose.
The dew sparkled on the grass.
"Good morning," said Rat, waking.
"Good morning," said Mole.
Toad was still sleeping and snoring.
"Well," said Rat, "there are chores to do."
Mole fed the horse and Rat got the dishes out.
Together they collected firewood.
Rat started a fire and Mole cooked breakfast.
Finally the smell of coffee woke Toad.
"Ah," said Toad, stretching. "Isn’t it great?
There are no chores to do on the road!"
"That’s true for people who sleep too late," grumbled Rat.
But Toad didn’t hear him.
He was too busy eating.
"I’m ready. Let’s go!" cried Toad after breakfast.
Mole and Rat got into the cart.
Toad tied the horse to the cart, and they started off.
The dusty road led through a meadow.
"Do you hear that noise?" asked Toad.
"It’s coming from behind us," said Mole.
They all looked.
A cloud of dust was coming up fast.
Vroom! Vroom!
"Oh no!" cried Rat. "Look out!"
A blast of wind zoomed past.
Vroom! Vroom!
"Ahh!" they screamed.
The cart tipped and fell over into a ditch.
The dust cleared.
Ahead, a big, beautiful car raced down the road!
The yellow cart lay on its side.
Pots and pans spilled onto the road.
Food was scattered on the grass.
"What a complete mess!" said Mole.
Rat jumped up and down.
"Crazy drivers!" shouted Rat.
"I’m going to call the police!"
"Look! The horse has run away," said Mole.
"The cart has a broken wheel," said Rat.
"I’ll go find the horse," said Mole.
"I’ll clean up this mess," said Rat.
Toad sat in the road staring after the car.
He had a big smile on his face.
"Vroom! Vroom!" said Toad.
"What?" said Rat.
"Vroom! Vroom! Vroom!" said Toad.
"Toad! What’s the matter with you?" said Rat.
Toad just sat in the middle of the road.
"Vroom! Vroom!" he said.
Rat put the broken wheel next to the cart.
He found the birdcage on the road.
It was upside-down.
"Poor birdie," Rat said.
Mole returned with the horse.
"What’s wrong with Toad?" Mole asked.
"He’s in some kind of dream," said Rat.
"I wish he would help clean up."
Toad slowly lifted his arm.
He pointed at the far-off cloud of dust.
"Now that’s the real way to travel!" shouted Toad.
"In a car!"
"A car!" shouted Toad. "Of course!"
He danced in circles.
"I must have one! Vroom!
Why have I waited so long?"
"Help me," cried the bird in the cage.
"You’ll be all right," said Mole to the bird.
"Let’s set the cart right," said Mole.
Rat and Mole tried to push the cart up.
"One, two, three, push!" they said.
The cart was too heavy.
"One more try," said Mole.
"Toad," said Rat, "please help with the cart."
"It’s just a silly yellow cart," said Toad.
"Who cares? Soon I will have a car!"
"What can we do with him?" asked Mole.
"Nothing," said Rat. "He found a new interest.
He’ll be like this for days."
"Vroom! Vroom!" shouted Toad.
Rat and Mole decided to leave the cart.
"The wheel is broken anyway," said Rat.
"We’ll walk to the next town," said Mole.
Rat carried the birdcage and Mole led the horse.
"Vroom!" said Toad. He ran to catch up.
"Don’t worry," he said cheerfully.
"We’ll find a stable for the horse.
Then we’ll take a train home. Zip zip!"
The next day the riverbank was quiet.
Rat and Mole sat fishing by the water.
A rabbit ran up. "Did you hear the news?" she said.
"Toad has bought a big fancy car!"
News of Toad’s new car faded.
The days got shorter and summer faded too.
Soon the river was too cold for boating.
Winter was on its way.
"You slept late, Rat," Mole said one morning.
"It’s cold," said Rat. "There isn’t much to do.
I think I’ll write poems by the fire."
This was Rat’s favorite hobby in winter.
But Mole was bored.
"Let’s invite Badger to dinner," Mole said.
"I only saw him once, and it was very quick.
He seems so odd and strange!"
"Oh, Badger hates dinner parties," said Rat.
"Maybe he would come for tea?" asked Mole.
"He’s very shy," said Rat.
"He will visit when he’s ready."
Every time Mole asked,
"Can we invite Badger today?"
Rat always answered the same way:
"Badger will show up sometime."
"Let’s go visit him," Mole said finally.
"Badger wouldn’t like that," said Rat.
"Anyway we can’t go, Mole," Rat explained.
"Badger lives in the Wild Wood."
"You said the folks there were nice," said Mole.
"Yes, but it’s a long way," said Rat.
"And the weather is much too cold."
Rat sat by the fire to write a poem.
Rat was sleepy.
Before long he was snoring in his chair.
Quietly Mole snuck out into the cold.
Feeling brave, he hurried to the Wild Wood.
The trees in the Wild Wood looked twisted.
Mole followed a trail between the trees.
The branches were leafless. Logs tripped him.
Twigs cracked under his feet.
"It's very gloomy
and dark," said Mole.
From holes in trees, evil faces peeked out.
Everywhere he looked, they stared!
"I must get off this path," said Mole.
Mole stepped off the trail, deep into the woods.
He heard a faint whistling.
"I should turn around," he said.
"There’s something up ahead."
Then the whistling was behind him.
"I don’t think I’ll turn around now," he said.
Mole stood there, cold and afraid.
"I’m so alone," cried Mole.
Something made a pitter-patter sound.
"It sounds like falling leaves," Mole said.
"No, it sounds like little feet.
Are they in front or behind?"
The little feet were all around.
The footsteps grew louder—closer!
Suddenly a rabbit came running by.
He almost knocked Mole down.
The rabbit didn’t look back. He called back,
"Get out of here, you fool! Get out!"
"Oh no!" cried Mole. "Oh no!"
With his heart pounding, Mole ran.
He tripped over roots. He slipped on leaves.
Eventually he bumped into a hollow tree.
Mole was too tired to run anymore.
He crawled inside the hollow tree and hid.
While Mole shivered in the Wild Wood, Rat dozed.
Suddenly the fire crackled loudly.
Rat woke with a start.
The house was quiet.
"Mole! Moly!" Rat shouted. He got up.
"Mole’s hat is gone," he said.
"Mole’s boots are not by the door.
I bet he’s gone to the Wild Wood," Rat said.
Rat put on his coat.
He grabbed the biggest club from his closet.
"I hope Mole is safe," Rat said to himself.
Rat set out for the Wild Wood.
Inside the gloomy forest, wicked faces appeared.
But they disappeared when they saw Rat’s club.
"Moly, Moly, Moly! Where are you!
It’s me. It’s old Rat!" Rat called out.
Rat searched every trail in the woods.
"Mole must have left the path," he said.
"Well, that means I will too."
Rat stepped off the path.
Rat looked behind rocks.
He looked under piles of leaves.
Then he heard a faint, scared voice.
"Ratty?" the voice said. "Is that really you?"
Rat turned. Ahead was a hollow tree.
Rat went carefully to the tree and crept inside.
There was poor Mole, shaking with fear.
"Oh, Rat," Mole cried. "I’ve been so scared!"
Mole was shivering and tired. Rat patted him.
"I tried to warn you, Mole," said Rat.
"We Riverbankers never come here by ourselves."
"I’m sorry, Rat," cried Mole.
"It can be a dangerous place," said Rat.
"There are tricks for hiking in the Wild Wood."
"Tricks?" said Mole.
"You need to know certain words.
You need special plants to carry.
You need to know the sounds in the wood.
It’s easy if you know these things," said Rat.
"If you don’t, you can get into big trouble."
"I bet Toad comes here by himself," said Mole.
"Old Toad?" Rat laughed.
"He wouldn’t come here for a bag of gold!"
Mole was cheered by Rat’s laugh.
"Come on, then," said Rat. "It’s time to go home.
We can’t stay here at night. It’s too cold."
Rat poked his head out of the hollow tree.
"Oh no," said Rat.
"What’s up, Ratty?" asked Mole.
"Snow is up," replied Rat. "I mean down.
Snow is falling everywhere."
Mole looked out of the hollow.
The forest was covered in white.
Big white snowflakes filled the air.
"It’s beautiful," said Mole.
"Yes, you’re right," said Rat, sounding worried.
"The snow makes everything look different."
"What’s the matter?" asked Mole.
"Now even I can’t tell where we are!" said Rat.
Rat and Mole were lost in the forest.
It was cold, but they tried to be cheerful.
"I’ve seen that tree over there before," said Rat.
Then he shook his head. "No, I guess not."
"That round rock looks familiar," said Mole.
"Good for you, Mole," said Rat.
They walked over to a big rock.
"It’s not the one I thought," sighed Mole.
"We’ll find the way," said Rat. "Don’t worry."
But Rat knew they were in trouble.
All they could see was white snow and black trees.
They kept walking for hours.
"Let’s rest a minute," said Rat.
Rat sat down on a fallen tree.
They were tired, hungry, and very cold.
"We can’t stay here long," said Mole.
"The snow will get too deep."
Mole held out his hand for his friend.
Rat took it. "Thank you," he said, and stood.
They walked a little further.
"Look, Mole," said Rat.
"There’s a small valley ahead of us.
Maybe it has a dry place where we can rest."
"That’s a good idea," said Mole.
The wind blew hard and the snow fell thick.
The two friends went into the valley.
They searched for a dry hole or an empty cave.
Suddenly Mole tripped and fell.
"Ow! My leg!" he cried.
He held his leg in his paws.
It was bleeding.
"Ow! It hurts!" cried Mole.
He was rolling in the snow, holding his leg.
"Poor Mole," said Rat kindly. "Let me look."
Mole sat still, and Rat bent down.
"Well, you really hurt yourself," said Rat.
"I tripped over a stump," cried Mole.
"But it’s a clean cut," said Rat.
"It looks like you hit something sharp, like metal."
"It hurts!" cried Mole.
Rat tied up Mole’s cut with his handkerchief.
"Hmm, metal," said Rat. "I wonder."
Rat started scratching in the snow.
"What are you doing?" asked Mole.
Rat didn’t answer, but he dug harder.
"Hey!" cried Mole. "What’s going on?"
Suddenly Rat stood. He held something in his hand.
"What did you find, Ratty?" asked Mole.
"Come and see!" said Rat.
Mole walked over to have a look.
"It looks like a broken door knocker," said Mole.
"What does that tell you?" asked Rat.
"Uh, nothing," said Mole.
"Oh, stop standing there!" cried Rat. "Dig!"
Rat clawed at the snow.
White flakes flew all around him.
"Why are you so excited?" asked Mole.
Rat just kept digging, so Mole dug too.
"I don’t know what we’re digging for," said Mole.
"It was just an old door knocker."
Suddenly Rat stopped. "Look at this!" he shouted.
Mole looked. There was something under the snow.
Rat brushed at the snow.
He cleared away an area of painted wood.
"What is it?" said Mole, excited.
"Never mind," said Rat. "Now we must really dig."
They scraped and dug and pushed away the snow.
At last the entire piece of wood was cleared.
In the moonlight, Mole saw what it was.
"Why, it’s a little door!" cried Mole.
An iron bell hung beside the door.
"Read this, Mole," said Rat, pointing.
A name was carved in the center of the door:
MR. BADGER.
Mole fell backward in the snow.
"Rat!" he cried with surprise.
"It’s Mr. Badger’s house!
You have a very clever brain, Ratty!"
"How did you figure it out?" asked Mole.
"Are you going to talk all night?" said Rat.
"Ring that bell!"
Mole grabbed the bell rope.
He pulled so hard his feet left the ground.
Rat beat the door with his club.
"I hope he comes soon!" cried Mole.
They waited.
They stamped their feet to keep warm.
At last Rat said, "I think I hear footsteps."
They heard someone unlock the door.
The door opened a few inches.
A long nose poked out.
Two sleepy eyes stared at them.
Rat and Mole waited for the door to open.
But it didn’t open any further.
"Who woke me up?" cried an angry voice.
"Can’t a badger get some sleep?"
"Oh, Badger," said Rat.
"Let us in. It’s Rat, and my friend Mole.
We lost our way in the snow."
Suddenly the door swung wide open.
"Why Ratty! Come on in!" cried Badger.
"Lost in the Wild Wood?
My friends, you are soaking wet!"
Badger quickly shut the door behind them.
Badger wore a long dressing gown.
On his feet were large slippers.
He held a candle in his paw.
"Thank you, Mr. Badger," said Mole.
Badger looked kindly at Rat and Mole.
"Come into the kitchen," he said.
"There’s a fire and some supper too."
Badger led them down a long hallway.
"I am so hungry!" Mole said to Rat.
"Me too!" agreed Rat.
"Here we are," said Badger.
He held open the door to a cozy kitchen.
"Sit by the fire," Badger told them.
"Take off those wet coats. Boots too!"
Badger gave them robes and slippers to wear.
"Now let me get you some dinner."
Badger brought them plates of hot food.
Soon they were warm and dry.
Mole looked at Badger’s friendly face.
"I have finally met Badger," thought Mole.
Rat and Mole ate in Badger’s warm kitchen.
No one spoke until the plates were empty.
"We’re sorry that we bothered you," said Rat.
"I’m glad to help," said Badger.
Badger gave them some tea.
"Now tell me," said Badger. "How is Toad?"
Rat was surprised.
Normally Badger did not talk about Riverbankers.
"How’s Toad?" said Rat. "Not good."
"He crashed another car last week," said Mole.
"He’s a very bad driver," said Rat.
"But he thinks he’s the best in the world."
"How many has he had?" asked Badger.
"Do you mean crashes or cars?" asked Mole.
"It’s the same thing," laughed Rat.
"Seven! His yard is full of broken cars."
"He went to the hospital three times," said Mole.
"Soon he’ll run out of money!" said Rat.
"Or he’ll get killed!"
"Shouldn’t we do something?" said Mole.
Badger rubbed his chin.
"The other animals will have to help.
But we must wait until spring," he said.
"In winter all the animals are too sleepy."
Rat and Mole nodded.
"I’m sleepy," said Rat. "It’s time for bed."
"I’m sleepy too," yawned Mole.
"Come along," said Badger.
Badger led them to their beds.
Badger was right.
In winter animals can’t do anything too active.
The whole riverbank was worried.
"Rat was away all night," said a squirrel.
"Mole is gone too," said a robin.
"Maybe they went to the Wild Wood!" said a deer.
When Otter heard, he was worried too.
"Can you find them?" asked the squirrel.
"I’ll look for Badger’s house," Otter told them.
"When animals get in trouble, he often helps."
The Wild Wood was cold and empty.
Otter found no one to ask for news.
Then he saw a rabbit hopping by.
"Did you see my friend Mole?" asked Otter.
"Ahh!" screamed the rabbit, turning around.
"You scared me!"
"Have you seen Mole?" Otter said again.
"Well . . . ," said the rabbit. "Why do you ask?"
"Don’t play games," said Otter. "Did you see him?"
Otter hit the rabbit on the head.
"Ow!" cried the rabbit, rubbing his head.
"You mean Rat’s friend."
The rabbit laughed.
"I told all the other rabbits.
They thought it was very funny.
Mole got lost, and he was soo scared!"
"Why didn’t you do something?" Otter asked.
"Like what?" asked the rabbit.
"Take him in! Help him!" said Otter.
"What? Us?" said the rabbit, confused.
"You expect us rabbits to help anyone?"
Shaking his head, Otter hurried on.
In the morning, Rat and Mole slept late.
They got up and went to Badger’s kitchen.
Two little hedgehogs were eating breakfast.
The hedgehogs stood and bowed.
"Please sit down," said Rat, yawning.
"Why are you here?" asked Mole.
"We were on our way to school,"
said the older hedgehog.
"Mother made us go," said the younger hedgehog.
"She always makes us go."
"Even in a storm," said the older hedgehog.
"And?" said Rat, breaking eggs into a pan.
"We got lost," said the older hedgehog.
"We saw Badger’s door and knocked."
Suddenly the doorbell clanged.
Billy, the younger hedgehog, answered the door.
Noisy stomping came from the hall.
"What’s all the excitement about?" said Mole.
Then Otter burst into the kitchen.
He jumped on Rat and hugged him.
"Here you are!" shouted Otter.
"Get off me!" yelled Rat.
Rat’s mouth was full of toast.
Otter let go, and Rat coughed.
"The whole riverbank is worried," said Otter.
"Nobody knows where you two went!"
"Did they send you to look for us?" asked Mole.
"Of course!" said Otter.
Otter gave Mole a hug too.
Badger heard the noise and came from his study.
"Hello, Otter," he said. "Is it still snowing?"
"Just a few flakes," said Otter.
"Okay, boys, time to go home," Badger said.
Billy and his brother put on their mittens.
"Good-bye!" cried the hedgehogs.
After they left, Rat and Otter sat together.
They loved to talk about the river.
"I love your home," Mole said to Badger.
"It’s so much like my own."
Badger took some bacon from the pan.
"An underground home is always safe," he said.
"Oh yes," Mole agreed.
"Nothing can happen to you," said Badger.
"And if your house is too small . . . "
"You just dig a little," said Mole, smiling.
"Come. I’ll show you!" cried Badger.
"Right this way."
Badger took a lantern from the wall.
He went down a hallway.
Mole jumped out of his chair and followed.
Badger showed Mole many rooms and hallways.
"Look at all the rooms you have!" said Mole.
He was amazed by the size of Badger’s home.
"This room is as big as Toad Hall," Mole said.
The next room was as small as a closet.
Each hallway led to more rooms.
"Incredible! How did you do all this?" asked Mole.
"I didn’t do it," said Badger.
"You didn’t?" asked Mole, confused.

26.title: The Story of the Wild Wood

paragraphs.text: Badger and Mole stopped.
They stood in one of Badger’s many tunnels.
Some of the wall was brick.
There were stone arches overhead.
"You didn’t build it?" said Mole.
"What do you mean?"
"The Wild Wood was once a city," said Badger.
"People walked, talked, and slept here."
"People?" asked Mole.
"Yes," said Badger.
"They built a grand city with towers and walls.
They thought it would last forever."
"What happened to them?" asked Mole.
"Who knows?" said Badger.
"People come, stay for a bit, and go.
That is their way, but animals remain."
"What happened to the city?" asked Mole.
"Plants grew in the empty streets," said Badger.
"The buildings fell, and trees took root.
Soon soil covered the stones."
"And the animals came back?" asked Mole.
"Yes," said Badger.
"The Wild Wood was full of animals again.
When I came, I just dug out the rooms I needed."
"But why is the Wild Wood so scary?" asked Mole.
"Well," said Badger, "there are all kinds of animals.
Some are good, and some are bad."
Mole thought of the faces in the wood.
"I know," he said with a shiver.
"Don’t worry," said Badger. "You’re my friend.
I’ll tell them all not to bother you again."
Mole and Badger returned to the kitchen.
Rat was walking up and down in his coat.
"I want to get back to my river," said Rat.
"But, Rat," said Mole, "Badger’s home is lovely."
Rat really wanted to leave.
"I can’t stay underground this long!
Come on, Mole!" Rat said.
"We must go before it gets dark."
"Don’t worry, Rat," said Otter.
"I know every path in the Wild Wood.
I can lead you home at night."
"But I want to go now!" yelled Rat.
"All right," said Mole.
"Let me put on my hat and boots."
"You can use my shortcut," said Badger.
"You won’t need to walk through the Wild Wood."
Badger took his lantern and led the way.
Otter came too.
The dark tunnel seemed to go on forever.
Finally Rat cried, "I see daylight!"
"Here we are," said Badger, at the tunnel opening.
He pushed them through and waved good-bye.
Otter piled some leaves to hide the hole.
Just behind them was the Wild Wood.
Mole looked at it and shivered.
"I’m glad I’m out of there!" he said.
"Well, I’m going home!" cried Otter.
And he ran down a trail.
The two friends started home.
Suddenly Mole stopped and sniffed.
Something smelled safe and familiar.
"Oh Ratty, please stop! Wait!" cried Mole.
But Rat kept walking.
"Ratty! Please stop!" shouted Mole again.
But Rat was far ahead.
"It’s my old home!" cried Mole.
"I must go there!"
Rat didn’t turn back.
"Hurry up, Mole," Rat called without looking.
"Oh, please come back!" yelled Mole.
He stood in the road alone.
Mole’s home was nearby.
"Should I go home?" he wondered.
"Or should I go with my friend?"
The choice made his heart ache.
With a sigh, Mole ran after Rat.
Finally Mole caught up.
"Won’t it be great to sit by the fire?" asked Rat.
"Sure," said Mole, dragging his feet.
Rat turned and looked at Mole.
"Mole, you’re tired. Sit down," said Rat.
Mole sat on a fallen log.
His lips trembled, and he burst into tears.
"What is it, Mole?" asked Rat, surprised.
"I know it’s not cozy like your house," sobbed Mole.
"Or grand like Toad Hall. But it was mine!"
"What was yours?" asked Rat.
"I went away and forgot all about it," cried Mole.
"Then I smelled it again."
"But what did you smell?" Rat asked.
"My home!" sobbed Mole.
"It was my old home!
And you wouldn’t turn back!"
Rat sat beside Mole on the log.
"When I c-c-called you," cried Mole,
"you w-w-wouldn’t listen."
Rat patted Mole on the shoulder.
"You d-d-didn’t turn back.
I h-h-had to leave it," cried Mole.
"I only wanted to see my home again!"
"I’ve been so selfish!" said Rat.
"I only cared about my home by the river."
Mole wiped his tears.
"Well," said Rat, "we’re going to find your home."
Rat stood up. "Come along," he said.
"Show me the way."
"Oh Ratty, it’s no good," said Mole.
"It will be dark soon."
"We will find your place," Rat said.
"Even if we stay out all night."
Rat took Mole’s arm, and they walked back.
"I think I smell it, Rat," said Mole.
Mole stopped and raised his nose.
"Well?" asked Rat, excited.
Mole sniffed his way across a field.
He ran this way and that.
"Have you found it, Mole?" asked Rat.
Suddenly Mole dived.
"Where did he go?" said Rat.
Mole poked his head out of a small tunnel.
"It’s down here!" Mole said.
Rat dived right behind him.
Down the dark tunnel they went!
Rat and Mole wiggled through the dark tunnel.
Before long it got bigger, and they stood up.
Mole struck a match.
He lit a lantern hanging from the wall.
"Here we are," said Mole.
They stood in front of a little door.
A sign on it read: Mole End.
"So this is your home," said Rat.
Mole opened the door.
He stepped in holding the lantern.
"What a perfect home!" cried Rat, laughing.
"Everything is so tidy and pleasant."
Mole pointed things out.
"These are my plants and pictures," he said.
"This is my glass ball."
Mole smiled as Rat looked at his things.
Then Mole let out a cry.
"Oh no, dust! It’s everywhere!
It’s on everything," he said.
"I was away from home too long."
Mole sat at his table feeling sad again.
"Oh Ratty, why did I bring you here?" he said.
"It’s so small and dirty."
"But your little place has everything!" said Rat.
"Well, I don’t have any food," cried Mole.
"Don’t worry," said Rat. "We’ll find something."
Rat busily searched the cupboards.
"Tuna!" yelled Rat, holding up a can.
"Biscuits!" he shouted, opening a bread box.
"It will be a great dinner, Mole," Rat said.
"All we need is a warm fire!"
Rat put the tuna and biscuits on the table.
"I can’t wait to eat!" said Rat.
He busily piled wood in the stove.
"I remember now," said Mole, jumping up.
Mole opened a bottom cupboard.
"I left some sausage in here!" said Mole.
Rat set a frying pan on the stove.
"Put that right here, Moly!" said Rat, grinning.
Mole put the sausage in the pan.
"How did you get such a nice place?" asked Rat.
"Well, my aunt left me the house," said Mole.
"Wonderful!" cried Rat.
"And I got my plants from the swamp," said Mole.
"Very nice," said Rat.
"And I bought the pictures myself," said Mole.
Mole set the table as he talked.
Rat brought the frying pan to the table.
"And your glass ball?" asked Rat.
"Someone threw that out," grinned Mole.
"Can you believe it?"
"Well, you know what they say," said Rat.
"One person’s trash . . . "
"Is another person’s treasure!" laughed Mole.
They heard a noise outside.
"Who’s that?" asked Rat.
Mole listened and heard tiny voices at his door.
"I think it’s the field mice," said Mole happily.
"They sing carols at this time of year."
"Well, let me see them!" shouted Rat.
He jumped up and ran to the door.
Rat’s cheerfulness made Mole smile.
Mole and Rat opened the door.
Outside, ten young field mice stood in a line.
"What fine boys!" said Rat.
"What colorful red mufflers!" cried Mole.
The mice looked up with bright eyes.
An older mouse held up a lantern.
"Now, one, two, three!" he cried.
Together, their tiny voices rose in the air.
Let your doors open wide.
Even with the snow outside,
Bring us in by the fire.
You will have joy in the morning!
Here we stand in the cold and sleet,
Frozen fingers and frozen feet.
You by the fire, bring us in from the street.
You will have joy in the morning!
The mice ended their song and smiled.
"Very well sung!" cried Rat.
"Ah, listen!" said Mole. "The bells!"
Church bells rang in the distance.
"Now come on in. All of you!" said Rat.
"Yes, come in!" said Mole, smiling.
"This is just like old times.
I always give the mice a feast after they sing."
The field mice all hurried inside.
They stood by the fire, warming their paws.
Mole was suddenly upset.
"Rat," he said, "we have nothing to give them!"
"I'll take care of it!" said Rat.
Rat pointed to the older mouse with the lantern.
He was the choir leader.
"Come here," Rat said. "I want to talk to you."
The choir leader came over to Rat.
"Can I help you, sir?" said the mouse.
Rat spoke quietly.
"Are the shops still open?" he asked.
The mouse nodded politely.
"Shops are open late this time of year," he said.
Rat put some coins into the mouse’s paw.
"Great!" said Rat. "Go buy us some good food."
The rest of the mice sat down by the fire.
Mole was opening his empty cupboards.
"Oh dear," Mole said, shaking his head.
"Now," cried Rat, "what shall we do for fun?"
Mole turned and looked at Rat.
"Well," said Mole, "these mice are actors too.
They did a play about pirates last year."
"Really? Let’s see!" cried Rat.
The mice whispered together.
"Samuel should do it," said one, pointing.
"Yes, Sammy will do it!" said the others.
One young mouse stood shyly.
"Say something from the play," said Rat.
"Ahem," said Samuel.
"Go on," said Mole.
"Don’t be shy," said Rat.
"Um, um . . . ," Samuel said.
The other mice encouraged him.
"You can do it, Sammy!" they said.
"Um, um," the young mouse repeated.
"Here now, little one," said Rat.
"Everyone is waiting."
"Oh Rat," said Mole, "give him a chance."
Suddenly the door flew open.
Everyone turned to look at the door.
"What’s this?" said Mole.
A big basket of food stumbled in.
The basket tipped this way and that.
Then Mole saw the choir leader under it.
"He can’t carry that much!" Mole yelled.
Finally shy little Samuel said something.
"Look out!" he shouted.
The basket spilled, and food rolled across the floor.
Surprised, Mole looked around.
"Pudding! Jam! Turnips! Potatoes! Candy!
Where did it all come from?" said Mole.
"The play is over!" shouted Rat.
"Pick up the food!"
All the mice scattered.
"I got an apple!" cried one mouse.
"Here are some carrots!" cried another.
Two mice fought over a piece of candy.
Rat gave directions to every mouse:
"Get the butter dish!
Don’t forget the napkins!
Who has the forks?"
Soon supper was ready.
Mole took his seat at the head of the table.
The mice sat on both sides.
Rat sat at the other end.
"I can’t believe it," sighed Mole.
"What a happy homecoming this is!"
"Let’s eat!" cried Rat, with his fork held high.
"Dig in!" cried Rat.
Everyone around the table started to eat.
No one was shy about passing plates.
All the food was tasty.
"Hey, Mole," said one little mouse.
"Did you hear about the swamp?"
"No," said Mole. "What happened?"
"It dried up," another mouse answered.
"Hey, Mole," said a mouse.
"Do you remember Beaver’s house?"
"Of course," said Mole.
"It’s twice as big now," said the choir leader.
Mole laughed. "Good old Beaver!
He never stops building."
All through dinner, Rat did not say much.
He just smiled and ate.
"Well, it’s time to go," said the choir leader.
Mole gave his visitors a warm good-bye.
The mice left with pockets full of treats.
As they went out the door, they sang.
You opened your doors so wide.
We left the snow outside.
You brought us in by the fire.
You will have joy in the morning!
You will have joy in the morning!
You will have joy in the morning!
Rat and Mole watched them leave.
The mice’s lantern light faded behind the hill.
"Ratty, I’m going to bed," yawned Mole.
"Is it nice to be home?" asked Rat.
"Oh yes," sighed Mole.
"It’s also nice by the river with you."
"Ah, the river," said Rat.
"But I’m glad to have my home too," said Mole.
The long winter ended.
The bright sun made the riverbank green.
The river flowed and sparkled again.
It was finally spring!
Rat and Mole planned to go boating.
"But first, breakfast!" said Rat, as he ate his egg.
Mole finished his toast and jelly.
They heard a knock at Rat’s door.
"Mole, I’m still eating," said Rat.
"Will you answer the door?"
"Sure," said Mole.
Mole ran to the door and opened it.
"Mr. Badger!" cried Mole.
Rat dropped his fork.
"Badger? Here?" said Rat.
"He hardly ever leaves the Wild Wood!"
Badger walked into the room.
"The hour has come!" said Badger.
Mole looked at the clock on the wall.
"What hour?" asked Mole.
"You should say whose hour!
It is the hour for Toad!" cried Badger.
"What?" asked Rat, scratching his head.
"Winter is over," said Badger.
"We must take care of Toad!"
"Hooray!" shouted Mole.
He jumped up and down. "When?"
"Right now!" said Badger.
"Toad just bought another big car!"
"Oh no," said Rat, getting up from the table.
"We must get to Toad Hall," cried Mole.
"Before it’s too late!" added Rat.
The three friends rushed out the door.
Together they set out for Toad Hall.
Badger, Rat, and Mole arrived at Toad Hall.
"Badger was right," said Mole. "Look at that."
A shiny car was parked at the house.
It was painted red—Toad’s favorite color.
"It sure is big," said Rat.
"I’ll knock on the door," said Badger.
But before he could, the door burst open.
"Hello!" shouted Toad, smiling.
Toad wore long gloves and a coat.
Goggles covered his eyes.
"You are just in time!" said Toad.
"It’s time for a ride in my new car!"
The three friends stared at him.
"What a silly outfit!" said Rat.
"What’s wrong?" said Toad.
"These are my driving clothes."
"Take him inside," said Badger.
Rat and Mole grabbed Toad.
"Hey, let go of me!" yelled Toad.
He kicked his legs in the air.
They dragged Toad back into his house.
"Now then," Badger said to Toad,
"take off those stupid clothes!"
"I will not!" cried Toad proudly. "I won’t!"
"Boys, take off his things!" Badger said.
The three friends went right to work.
"I’ll sit on him," said Rat.
"Here, I’ve got his gloves," said Mole.
"I’ve got his goggles," said Badger.
They pulled at his cap and coat.
Toad kicked angrily.
"Ahhh!" screamed Toad. "What are you doing?"
Toad struggled under his friends.
"Get off me!" he screamed.
"You have no right! Help! Help!"
"Hold still, Toad," said Mole.
Finally they got Toad out of his coat and cap.
The goggles and gloves lay on the floor.
"Now stand up, Toad," said Mole.
"You look like yourself again."
Toad calmed down.
In fact, he even giggled a little.
"Toad, you knew we would come," said Badger.
"We warned you!" said Rat.
"You are spending all your money," said Mole.
"But . . . ," said Toad.
"You are getting a bad name," said Badger.
"But . . . ," said Toad.
"The police are always after you," said Rat.
"But . . . ," said Toad.
"You are a terrible driver!" cried Mole.
Toad looked down sadly.
"Toad, we don’t think you’re bad," said Rat.
"But you must give up your cars," said Badger.
"Then everything will be right again," said Mole.
Badger put his hand on Toad’s shoulder.
"Let’s go into the next room," he said.
"We won’t come out until you make a promise.
You must promise to stop driving."
Badger led Toad into the next room.
He closed the door.
"It’s useless," sighed Rat.
"Talking does nothing. Toad will say anything!"
Rat and Mole sat in armchairs in Toad Hall.
In the next room, Badger was talking to Toad.
"I hope Toad is taking it well," said Mole.
"I don’t think Toad will listen," said Rat.
They heard Badger’s voice go quiet.
"Rat, it sounds like Toad is crying," said Mole.
The door opened, and Badger and Toad appeared.
Badger looked serious and Toad looked tearful.
"Sit down, Toad," said Badger.
Toad sat next to Rat and Mole.
Badger faced them and cleared his throat.
"My friends, Toad is truly sorry," said Badger.
"Well, that’s good news," said Mole.
"Toad," said Badger, "I want you to apologize."
Toad looked this way and that.
The others waited in silence.
Suddenly, Toad jumped up.
"No! I’m not sorry!" yelled Toad.
"I won’t stop driving! Vroom!"
"What?" shouted Badger. "You promised . . . "
Toad pointed at the room. "I promised in there.
You were so angry," Toad said, "and I felt bad.
But out here , I changed my mind."
"I told you, didn’t I?" said Rat to Mole.
"Well," said Badger, "there’s only one thing to do.
You won’t change your ways.
So we’ll stay here until you do!"
Rat, Mole, and Badger grabbed Toad.
They dragged him upstairs.
They locked him in his bedroom.
"Let me out!" shouted Toad.
Badger put the bedroom key in his pocket.
Toad looked out the keyhole.
"Open the door!" screamed Toad.
"You can’t lock me in here!"
"Calm down, Toad," said Rat.
Mole said, "We’ll look after everything."
"Your money won’t be wasted!" said Badger.
"Let me out!" yelled Toad.
"No more police," said Rat.
"Let me out!" yelled Toad.
"No more hospitals," said Mole.
"Let me out!" yelled Toad.
Toad’s three friends went downstairs.
"Toad is still screaming," said Mole.
"We must guard him every minute," said Badger.
"I’ll take the first watch," said Rat.
Badger and Mole left Rat with the key.
They went outside to put the car away.
Upstairs, Toad moved four chairs.
He set them up like the seats of a car.
"I’m going for a drive anyway!" yelled Toad.
"Vroom!" said Toad, sitting in a seat.
"I'm speeding!" said Toad, leaning forward.
"Watch out!" cried Toad, pretending to crash.
Toad flipped forward and fell on the floor.
"What fun!" he said, and he did it again.
Crash, flip, thud! Crash, flip, thud!
Rat ran upstairs.
"Are you all right?" asked Rat through the door.
"Rat," moaned Toad, "get me a doctor.
I hit my head.
I may not live much longer."
"I’m dying," cried Toad from his room.
"Get me a doctor, please! "Rat stood outside the door.
"Look, Toad," said Rat, "it can’t be that bad."
"Ohhhh," moaned Toad.
"Tomorrow you will say . . ."
"What? What?" asked Rat.
"You will say," Toad said sadly,
"‘If only I had done something!’"
Rat wasn’t sure what to do.
"I’m not supposed to leave Toad," thought Rat.
"Ohh," moaned Toad.
"But what if he’s really sick?" Rat asked himself.
"I’m dying, Rat," said Toad.
"Say good-bye to everyone for me."
"I’d better get a doctor," thought Rat.
"Just to be safe."
"I’ll be right back, Toad," said Rat. "Hang on!"
Rat ran downstairs and out the door.
Toad got up at once and put on his best suit.
He opened a drawer to get some money.
"Just a little cash," said Toad to himself.
He stuffed his pockets with bills.
"Let me see," said Toad. "Ah, the way out!"
Toad knotted his sheets to make a rope.
He lowered himself out the window.
Toad sang a tune as he walked away.
I fooled Rat,
How wonderful is that?
I fooled Rat,
And that is that!
Toad hurried down the road.
"The sun is shining!" he said.
"I’m happy and carefree!"
Toad danced a little dance.
"Poor Ratty," Toad laughed.
"Badger will be so mad at him!
Rat’s a good friend.
But he isn’t as clever as Toad!"
Badger and Mole came back to Toad Hall.
Rat was very upset.
"Rat, what’s wrong?" asked Mole.
"Toad’s gone!" cried Rat. "I’m so stupid!"
"Toad said he needed a doctor," said Rat.
"He said he was dying."
"Oh Rat," said Badger.
"You fell for that old trick?"
Inside they found the bedroom empty.
"Never mind," said Badger. "We’ll see him again.
I just hope it’s not in the hospital."
"Or in jail," said Mole.
Down the road, Toad was eating at The Red Lion.
"What a yummy lunch!" said Toad to himself.
Then Toad heard his favorite sound.
Vroom! A big car drove up.
The driver and his friends got out.
Toad watched them come into the restaurant.
"They left the car alone," Toad thought happily.
"No one will mind if I look at it."
He walked out to the car.
"Oh my! It’s so beautiful," he gasped.
He looked around carefully.
No one was watching.
Outside the restaurant, Toad stared at the car.
"It has a big engine," said Toad.
He touched the car door.
His fingers trembled.
"Vroom," Toad said under his breath.
He kicked the tires lightly.
"What shiny wheels!" he said.
"They could handle any kind of road."
Without thinking, Toad hopped inside.
"Ohh, the seats are leather!" he cried.
Toad saw the key still in the car.
"I wonder what it sounds like?" thought Toad.
His hand shook as he reached out.
"Should I?" asked Toad.
Then he smiled. "Why not?
Just one little turn of the key."
Toad turned the key and the engine roared.
Vroom ! Vroom !
"I wonder how fast it goes," said Toad.
Toad drove out of the parking lot.
"It feels so good to drive again!" yelled Toad.
He stepped on the gas pedal.
Vroom !
Toad sped down the road.
He lost all thoughts of right and wrong.
"Toad the Road Warrior!
Lord of the Trail!" yelled Toad.
"I am King of the Road!"
He didn’t know where he was going.
He didn’t care who saw him.
Only one thing mattered.
He was driving again!
Rap ! Rap ! Rap !
The judge pounded his desk.
Toad stood with his head bowed.
Everyone in the court looked angry.
"Clerk!" the judge yelled.
"Mr. Toad is the worst criminal I know.
How long can we lock him up?"
"Let me see," said the clerk.
"He stole a car.
He drove very dangerously.
He was rude to the police."
"My friends know I’m not terrible," thought Toad.
But Toad’s friends were not there.
"Let me add everything up," said the clerk.
"His penalty is twenty years."
"Excellent!" cried the judge. "Take him away!"
The police chained Toad’s hands and feet.
"Come with us," said a policeman.
They dragged him from the court.
Outside, a crowd shouted at Toad.
"Troublemaker!" said a beaver.
"Car thief!" screamed a chipmunk.
"Bandit!" yelled a skunk.
Children shouted at Toad and sang:
Look at Toad!
He hit the road!
Now he’s going to jail!
They dragged Toad to a dark dungeon.
A jailer stood by with a ring of keys.
"Oh no!" cried Toad.
The jailer pushed Toad in and the door clanged shut.
Mole lay on the riverbank.
Rat was away visiting Otter.
"Oh, why didn’t I go with Rat?" said Mole.
"He’s late, and now the sun is setting."
At last Mole heard Rat’s footsteps.
Rat sat down beside him.
"Why did you stay so long?" asked Mole.
"I had to," said Rat. "Otter is in trouble."
"What is it?" asked Mole.
"Otter’s son, Little Portly," said Rat.
"He’s missing again."
"Oh, Portly is always running off," said Mole.
"I know," said Rat.
"And he always comes back," said Mole.
"But Portly has been missing for days," said Rat.
Mole listened closely to Rat’s news.
"Otter looked everywhere," said Rat.
"He asked every animal.
No one saw Little Portly anywhere."
"What will Otter do?" asked Mole.
"Otter goes to the old bridge," said Rat.
"He taught Portly to swim there.
Portly caught his first fish there too."
"It’s a place Portly remembers," said Mole.
"Yes, Portly loves the old bridge," said Rat.
"Otter waits there every night."
Rat and Mole sat quietly for a while.
They both imagined Otter at the bridge.
They thought of him worrying all night.
"Rat," said Mole, "we just can’t go to bed."
"I agree," said Rat. "Let’s find Portly."
Rat and Mole got the boat out.
It was dark now.
The moon shone on the water.
Rat rowed them onto the river.
"Our river looks so different at night," said Mole.
"It looks like silver," sighed Rat.
"I love my river at night."
"Let’s tie up here," said Mole.
He pointed to a willow tree.
"Yes, it’s a good place to start looking," said Rat.
The friends got out and searched.
"Nothing here," said Mole.
He looked in some hollow trees.
"Nothing here," said Rat.
He climbed out of a ditch.
They got back in the boat.
Mole paddled them down the river again.
A gentle wind came up.
It moved the reeds along the banks.
Rat sat up and said: "What’s that sound?"
"It’s only the wind in the reeds," said Mole.
"It’s music!" cried Rat. "Can’t you hear it?"
"No," said Mole.
"It’s gone," said Rat. "It was so beautiful.
It was like a song and a dream."
"I didn’t hear anything," said Mole.
"Oh!" said Rat. "I’ve never heard such music!"
"It’s just the wind in the reeds," said Mole.
"It’s the wind in the willows."
"The music is calling us, Mole!" cried Rat.
"We must follow it!"
Mole rowed carefully on.
Rat leaned forward, listening.
"What’s wrong with Rat?" thought Mole.
"He’s acting strange."
The river divided into two streams.
"Take the smaller stream," ordered Rat.
Mole steered the boat.
"The music is so clear," said Rat.
"Mole, you must hear it now!"
Suddenly Mole stopped rowing.
The music surrounded him.
"You hear it, Mole!" cried Rat.
"It’s magical!" said Mole.
"Row on, Mole!" said Rat.
Mole paddled forward again.
"Look at the grass and the trees," said Rat.
"Everything is glowing!" cried Mole.
"Look at the color of those roses!"
"Smell the wildflowers!" said Rat.
Ahead they saw a small island.
Willows grew all around it.
"Let’s tie up here," said Mole.
They got out of the boat.
Rat and Mole pushed through the willows.
"Strange," said Rat. "I feel happy, but also scared."
"I feel the same way," said Mole.
They stepped into a small, bright clearing.
"Dawn is coming," said Mole.
"Oh, the music stopped," said Rat.
Rat and Mole both looked up.
"Oh my!" cried Mole.
"Shh," said Rat gently.
A very strange sight appeared before them.
It was a strange creature.
He had the legs of a goat and the body of a man.
The horns on his head shone in the dawn.
His kind face had a soft beard.
"Rat, are you still afraid?" asked Mole.
"No," said Rat. "And yes.
He looks as strong as a thunderstorm."
"But as gentle as a summer breeze," said Mole.
"Look," said Rat. "He is holding pipes."
"The music!" said Mole quietly.
The kind face smiled at them.
"I think," said Rat, "he is a friend."
The dawn glowed, and a warm breeze touched them.
Then the two animals were alone.
For a moment they felt very sad.
"What did you say, Rat?" asked Mole.
He rubbed his eyes.
"I was just thinking," said Rat.
"Portly might be around here."
"Look!" said Mole. "There he is!"
Portly woke with a squeak of joy.
"Rat! Mole!" cried the little otter.
"You found me!"
Portly jumped into Mole’s arms.
But Rat stared at hoof marks in the sand.
"Some . . . big . . . animal was here," said Rat.
He tried to remember something, but couldn’t.
Mole carried Little Portly to the boat.
"Come along, Rat!" called Mole.
"Think of poor Otter.
He is waiting at the old bridge."
"Yeah! A ride on the river!" cried Portly.
Rat looked around at the small stream.
"Strange, it’s not as colorful as it was," he said.
Mole rowed them out to the main river.
When they reached the old bridge, the sun rose.
"Here we are," said Mole.
He lifted Portly out of the boat.
"Off you go, Portly," said Rat.
Portly ran up a path to the bridge.
"Daddy! Daddy!" shouted Portly.
"My little Portly!" called Otter.
Otter wrapped his lost son in his arms.
"It’s time to go home," said Rat.
Mole pushed the boat into the river.
"Do you hear the wind in the reeds?" asked Rat.
"It’s like music far away," said Mole.
"Can you hear the words to the music?" asked Rat.
"No, I can’t," said Mole.
"Then listen to me," said Rat.
"I’ll say them to you."
So my magic won’t turn
Your happiness to regret,
I’ll help you when you need me,
But then you’ll forget.
Mole listened.
For a moment he thought he heard the song.
"What do the words mean, Rat?" asked Mole.
But Rat was fast asleep.
Toad threw himself on the floor of the jail.
"This is the end!" cried Toad.
"I am finished!
I will be here forever."
The room was dark with shadows.
Water dripped: plink, plunk .
Creepy bugs crawled across the stones.
Toad jumped up and brushed his coat.
Toad shook the bars in the door.
"I was so stupid!" he yelled.
"Why didn’t I listen to Rat and Mole?
Oh Badger, you were so wise!"
The jailer’s daughter brought Toad his meals.
But Toad did not eat.
For days, he cried in the corner of his room.
The jailer’s daughter went to her father.
"Toad is so unhappy!" she said.
"He’s getting very thin!"
"My girl," said the jailer, "he’s a criminal.
You don’t have to care for him."
"He needs to eat!" she cried.
"I’ll make him a tasty meal."
"Do what you like," said her father.
"I’m tired of hearing him moan."
The daughter knocked on Toad’s door.
"Go away!" cried Toad.
"Stop crying," she said, and unlocked the door.
"I’ve brought you some dinner."
Toad smelled the food and lifted his head.
Then he remembered how angry he was.
"Leave me alone!" Toad yelled.
He cried by himself for the rest of the night.
The next morning, Toad was hungry.
He remembered the smell of the food.
"Things aren’t all that bad," he said.
"Crying without food won’t help me."
Toad stood and stretched his back.
"And I am very clever.
I am bold and fearless.
Trouble is just an adventure!" he said.
The jailer’s daughter knocked again.
"I have some tea and toast," she said.
"Come in!" Toad said cheerfully.
She put the tray in front of him.
"I’m so hungry!" cried Toad.
He grabbed the toast and ate.
"I’m glad you’re well," she said.
"Why don’t you tell me about your home?"
"Well, Toad Hall is famous," Toad began.
He sat back and drank his tea.
Toad enjoyed telling her all about himself.
"Are your friends nice?" she asked.
"They are the best in the world!" said Toad.
He told her about Badger, Rat, and Mole.
He talked to her about all the Riverbankers.
The jailer’s daughter visited every morning.
She enjoyed Toad’s friendship.
"What a shame," she thought.
"It’s not fair to lock him up."
One morning, she came to his room as usual.
"Hello," cried Toad cheerfully.
"Toad," she said with a serious look,
"do you want to get out of here?"
"Do you mean I can go home?" shouted Toad.
"Oh, I will sleep at Toad Hall again!"
Toad jumped up and down.
"Shh," the jailer’s daughter said.
She looked around.
"I have an aunt who is a washwoman.
My aunt does the prison wash," she said.
"What a hard job!" said Toad.
"And for the whole prison too!
Think of all the dirty clothes!"
"Quiet, Toad," the daughter said. "Listen!"
She continued, "Since you are rich . . ."
"Well, I am rich," said Toad.
"If you give her some money," she said,
"my aunt will give you her dress and bonnet."
"Why would I want her old dress?" said Toad.
"To escape!" she said.
"You can pretend to be her!"
Toad was surprised.
"Me? Dress like a washwoman?
I am Toad of Toad Hall!" said Toad.
He proudly shook his head.
The jailer’s daughter got angry.
"Maybe you can escape in a coach!" she shouted.
"A coach with four horses!"
She opened the door to leave.
"I’m sorry," Toad said. "You are so nice.
And I am a stupid toad."
The jailer’s daughter stopped.
"Introduce me to your aunt," said Toad.
That night, the jailer’s daughter returned.
Her aunt was with her.
The aunt carried a big bag.
"Here, Mr. Toad!" said the washwoman.
"I have your clothes."
"And here is something for you!" said Toad.
He gave her four gold coins.
The old woman opened the bag.
"Here’s my old dress and an apron," she said.
She gave Toad a shawl and a bonnet too.
"Now you must tie me up," said the washwoman.
"What?" asked Toad, surprised.
The washwoman explained.
"People will think you did it," she said.
"I don’t want them to know I helped you."
"What a wonderful idea!" said Toad.
"You are a very clever woman.
Everyone will think I’m dangerous!"
Toad tied up the washwoman.
"Now," said the jailer’s daughter,
"it’s your turn, Toad.
Take off your coat."
She helped Toad put on the dress and apron.
"Here’s the shawl," she said. "And the bonnet!"
Toad looked at himself.
"I don’t look so dangerous now," he said sadly.
"You look just like my aunt!" the daughter said.
"Will it work?" Toad asked.
"Just act like an old washwoman.
And don’t talk so much," said the jailer’s daughter.
"Good-bye, Toad," she said. "And good luck."
Toad walked through the dungeon.
His heart beat wildly.
"This is crazy," he thought.
"Someone will know it’s me."
Toad stepped out into a yard.
Across the yard was a gate.
"No one is stopping me!" thought Toad.
"Washwoman, you’re late today," said the guard.
"Here, I’ll unlock the door for you."
"It’s working!" thought Toad. "I fooled him!"
Another guard stood at the next gate.
"Give me a hug!" said the guard.
"You work so hard.
This prison is lucky to have you."
Toad was giggling under his bonnet.
He hugged the guard.
The last gate shut behind him.
He was free!
People waved as Toad walked through town.
"Hello, washwoman!" a squirrel called.
"Hello to you!" said Toad in a high voice.
A train whistle blew.
"A train!" cried Toad. "I’ll buy a ticket home!"
Toad ran to the station.
He hurried to the ticket window.
"One ticket to . . ." Toad said, out of breath.
Toad reached under his dress.
He had no pockets.
He had no money!
"Madam, hurry up and pay," said the ticket seller.
"Customers are waiting."
Toad turned around.
A long line waited behind him.
"Hurry up!" said a possum.
"Hey, we’re waiting!" yelled a turkey.
"I’m sure I have some money," said Toad.
Toad searched through his clothes again.
His shawl fell off, and he tore his dress.
"My money is in my coat," thought Toad.
"I left it in the jail!"
Toad smiled at the ticket seller.
"Just give me a ticket.
I’ll send you the money.
I’m rich and famous!"
Everyone behind him laughed.
"This washwoman is rich!" said the possum.
"And famous too!" said the turkey.
"Stand aside, lady," said the ticket seller.
A raccoon poked Toad from behind.
"My good woman," he said. "Make room."
Toad ran from the ticket window.
He sat on a bench and cried.
"I almost got a ticket for home!" he said.
"Soon the police will know I escaped.
They will hunt me down.
I’ll go back to jail."
Just then, a voice called out to him.
It was the train engineer.
"Hello lady!" he said. "What’s wrong?"
Toad looked up from the bench.
"Are you all right?" said the train engineer.
"You don’t look very happy."
"Oh, sir!" said Toad, crying.
"I am a poor washwoman.
I lost all my money."
"That’s awful," said the engineer.
"I can’t pay for a ticket," cried Toad.
"I must get home!"
"Do you have kids?" asked the engineer.
"Why, yes!" said Toad. "I have lots of kids.
They will be crying and hungry."
"Well, I’ll help you," said the engineer.
"You can wash my shirts to repay me."
"I will, as soon as I get home," said Toad.
"Hop up!" said the engineer.
"You can ride on the engine with me."
Toad thanked him and climbed up.
Toad didn’t know how to wash a shirt.
He wasn’t going to learn either.
"I’ll send him money," Toad thought.
"I’ll send enough to wash his shirts for a year!"
A flagman at the station waved a flag.
The engineer blew his whistle.
The train sped away.
Toad danced with delight.
"Soon I’ll be at Toad Hall!" Toad thought.
The engineer leaned out the side.
"I hear another train behind us!" he shouted.
"It’s chasing us, and it’s coming fast!"
Toad leaned out of the train.
He looked down the tracks.
A train was speeding after them.
"Stop! Stop!" yelled the riders on the train.
"They look like policemen!" said the engineer.
The police waved their clubs angrily.
Toad fell on his knees.
"Save me!" he cried. "Save me!"
"What?" asked the engineer.
"I am not a washwoman!" cried Toad.
"I do not have children!
I am Mr. Toad!"
The engineer was angry.
"Why are they chasing you?" he asked.
Embarrassed, Toad looked at him.
"I escaped from jail," said Toad.
"Why were you in prison?" said the engineer.
"It wasn’t serious," said Toad.
"I just borrowed a car.
But everyone got so upset about it."
"I should let them arrest you," said the engineer.
"But I don’t like policemen.
And I hate to see someone cry."
The engineer added coal to the fire.
"That will speed us up!" he said.
But the other engine sped up too.
"What am I going to do?" cried Toad.
"You will have to jump," said the engineer.
"What?" asked Toad, afraid.
The engineer slowed the train.
"Here’s your chance," he shouted. " Jump! "
Toad closed his eyes and jumped.
Toad jumped, bounced, and rolled down a hill.
Beside the tracks were some woods.
Toad ran and hid behind a tree.
The engineer’s train sped away.
"Here they come," Toad said to himself.
The policemen’s train zoomed past.
"And there they go!" he shouted.
Toad could hear the policemen.
"Stop! Stop!" they yelled.
"The clever Toad wins again!" Toad laughed.
He laughed so hard that tears ran down his face.
The sound of the trains disappeared.
Toad set out through the strange woods.
It was cold and getting dark.
"I wish I had something to eat," he said.
An owl flew by and bumped Toad’s arm.
"Hey!" cried Toad. "Don’t do that!"
"Who? Who? Who’s scared?" said the owl.
"Be quiet! I’m not scared," said Toad, shivering.
"Oh, washwoman!" a fox called after him.
"Your dirty dress needs a wash!"
"Get away!" yelled Toad.
He threw a stone, but the fox was gone.
Toad looked at his clothes.
"My dress is a mess," said Toad.
"My bonnet is torn."
He was bruised and covered in mud.
"Ow, my back aches," Toad moaned.
He sat down under a tree.
"I’m so tired," yawned Toad.
He lay down and fell right to sleep.
After many days of summer, the riverbank was busy.
Rat watched the birds packing their nests.
"Why do they have to fly south?" thought Rat.
"The riverbank is perfectly fine."
"Hey, Ratty!" called some mice. "Come and help."
They walked by carrying baskets and boxes.
"What are you up to?" asked Rat.
"Moving! To our winter home," said one mouse.
"But it’s a beautiful day," said Rat.
"Winter is far away."
"Oh, we know that," said another mouse.
"But we like to be ready!"
"Let’s go for a row," said Rat.
"We can have a picnic!"
"Not today, Rat!" said the first mouse.
"Ask another day, when no one is busy."
Rat frowned. "Fine! Do what you want!"
He turned and tripped over a box.
"Ow!" cried Rat, rubbing his back.
"Be more careful," said a bluebird.
"Be quiet," said Rat. "I don’t need any advice."
Birds flew around Rat’s head.
"What’s the hurry?" Rat yelled at them.
"We’re not going yet," said a robin. "But we will!"
"Why don’t you stay this year?" asked Rat.
"You always like it here."
"We have to go," said the bluebird.
"The south calls us!"
Before long, the mice and the birds were off.
Rat heard footsteps and turned around.
A visitor stood in the road.
It was a dusty rat in a sailor’s cap.
The dusty stranger bowed to Rat.
Then he smiled and sat down.
Rat sat down too.
The stranger took a deep breath.
"I smell clover and smoke on the wind.
A river runs close by here," he said, sniffing.
"You have a good life, my friend."
"Yes," said Rat proudly.
"The riverbank is the best!"
The visitor smiled to himself.
"Well, it’s not for everyone," he said.
"Where are you from?" asked Rat.
"I am a sea rat," he said.
"I was born in an old city far away."
"A sea rat?" asked Rat.
"Yes," said Sea Rat.
"I know every port in the world."
"You sail on big ships!" said Rat.
Rat loved all boats, big and small.
"Tell me all about it!" said Rat.
"Once I sailed the coast of Italy," said Sea Rat.
"I lived in the captain’s cabin."
Sea Rat sighed with pleasure.
"We ate shellfish with wine!
We dined on baked bread and cheese.
On shore, we lay under olive trees."
Rat imagined all the food.
"Now I’m hungry," said Rat.
"Will you have lunch with me?"
"A wonderful idea!" said Sea Rat.
Rat ran home to pack a picnic basket.
"Sea Rat will only eat the best!" said Rat to himself.
"I’ll put cheese and sausage in the basket.
Some bread too!"
Rat hurried back outside.
Sea Rat helped unpack the basket.
"This is excellent food!" cried Sea Rat.
While they ate, Sea Rat talked.
"Ah, my last trip was exciting," said Sea Rat.
"We sailed stormy seas.
A lighthouse guided us safely.
Then we rested on a sunny beach."
"What an adventure!" said Rat.
Sea Rat’s voice sounded magical.
"The sailors sang songs.
At night, we danced by the fire."
"Lovely!" cried Rat.
"In the morning, fishermen spread their nets.
Then we sailed for a secret island."
Rat listened as if he was dreaming.
"Now," said Sea Rat, "I am traveling south.
You should come with me."
"You’re right," said Rat, dreamily.
He went straight home to pack.
At home, Rat found his backpack.
He picked up his stick and coat.
"I will leave the riverbank," he mumbled.
"I will travel the wide seas."
Suddenly Mole appeared at his door.
"Where are you going, Ratty?" he asked.
"I’m going south," said Rat slowly.
"The sea is calling me."
Mole could not believe what he heard!
"Rat is leaving the riverbank?" he thought.
"Impossible!"
Mole looked into Rat’s eyes.
"Something is wrong!" Mole thought.
"Rat’s eyes are all red!"
Mole stood in the door to block Rat’s way.
"Let me go," said Rat.
He pushed at Mole to get by.
"I’m not letting you out, Rat!" cried Mole.
Mole grabbed his friend’s arms.
"Let me go," said Rat again.
The two friends struggled.
Mole threw his friend into a chair.
"You’re staying here!" yelled Mole.
Mole held Rat firmly.
Finally, Rat stopped struggling.
"Oh my, oh my," said Rat, bursting into tears.
"You’ll be all right," said Mole.
Mole locked the door.
He hung Rat’s coat on a hook.
Mole sat in a chair next to his friend.
"I’ll stay until you feel better," said Mole.
As Rat cried, he called out strangely:
"Secret islands! Shellfish!
Lighthouses! Sea songs!"
"What odd things he’s saying," Mole thought.
"I don’t know what he’s talking about."
Rat fell into a deep sleep.
"My poor friend," sighed Mole.
After a long sleep, Rat awoke.
He sat up in his chair.
"You look much better," said Mole.
Rat’s eyes were clear again.
"What happened to you?" asked Mole.
"You almost left the riverbank!"
"I don’t know," said Rat. "It’s hard to say."
Rat told Mole about the visitor.
"I listened to Sea Rat," said Rat.
"His story was like a dream.
I acted as if I wasn’t awake."
"How very strange," said Mole.
"Now, I feel sad," said Rat.
"Rat, you’ll be happy again," said Mole.
"Just look outside."
"Why?" asked Rat.
"The apples are red," said Mole.
"Nuts are falling from the trees.
The pumpkins are fat!"
"I’m feeling a little better," said Rat.
Mole went to get Rat’s notebook.
He found a pencil too.
"Here, Rat," said Mole.
"You haven’t written in a long time."
"I don’t want to," said Rat.
He pushed the notebook and pencil away.
"I’ll let you rest some more," said Mole.
Mole set the notebook on the table.
After Mole left, Rat picked up the pencil.
He sat with the notebook on his knee.
Then Rat started a new poem.
"Home Sweet Home," he wrote.
Toad woke up under a pile of leaves.
The sun shone in his eyes.
His toes were cold.
He sat up and yawned. "Where am I?"
Toad brushed the leaves from his dress.
Suddenly he remembered his escape.
"I’m free!" he cried. "I’m free! I’m free!"
Toad jumped up and down with joy.
"I need to find out where I am," said Toad.
Toad walked to a meadow nearby.
Beyond the meadow was a canal.
Beside the canal was a small path.
"Aha," said Toad, "here comes a horse."
A horse was walking on the path.
With a long rope, it pulled a boat on the canal.
"And here comes a boat," said Toad.
Before long, the boat was next to Toad.
A possum in a red bonnet steered the boat.
"Good morning, madam," yelled the possum.
"Good morning to you!" shouted Toad.
Toad walked beside the boat on the path.
"Where are you going?" the possum asked.
"I left my children to help a sick aunt," lied Toad.
"I lost all my money, and I can’t get home."
"Where do you live?" the possum asked.
"Near a fine house called Toad Hall," said Toad.
"Toad Hall? I’m going that way too!" she said.
"Hop in! I’ll take you there!"
Toad stepped onto the boat.
He felt very pleased with himself.
"Toad is lucky again!" he thought.
"I always win in the end!"
Toad stood on the boat.
He watched the countryside roll by.
"I’m finally on my way home!" he sighed.
The possum looked at Toad’s dress.
"So you’re a washwoman?" she asked.
"Oh yes," said Toad, remembering how he looked.
Then he could not stop himself. He started to brag.
"I have the best business in the country!
The richest people bring me their clothes!
And twenty washwomen work for me," said Toad.
"I’m very impressed!" said the possum.
"I just love doing the wash," said Toad.
"When I’m washing, I feel great!
I clean clothes better than anyone."
"How lucky that I met you!" said the possum.
"What do you mean?" asked Toad.
"My dirty clothes are in the back," she said.
"They need washing."
"Oh, why didn’t I keep quiet?" thought Toad.
"There’s a tub and some soap too," she said.
"But, but . . . ," said Toad.
"It will take a while to get to Toad Hall," she said.
"You can enjoy yourself on the way!"
"Let me steer for you," said Toad.
"You must be tired of steering.
Then you can do the washing."
"No, no," she said. "You go have some fun!"
"I don’t know how to wash," thought Toad.
"What are you waiting for?" asked the possum.
Then Toad thought, "Oh, I’m sure it’s easy.
Anyone can wash clothes!"
Toad walked to the back of the boat.
"I’m Toad of Toad Hall!" he grumbled.
"I don’t wash clothes!"
Beside the dirty clothes was a washtub.
Toad picked up the soap.
He held up a shirt.
"How do I wash this?" he said.
He dipped it in the tub.
"Should I rub soap on it?" he asked.
Toad laid the shirt on the deck.
"Okay, I’ll rub some soap on it," said Toad.
"Hmmm, now what do I do?"
"Oh, I’ll dip it in the tub again!" said Toad.
Toad put the shirt in the water.
"Hmmm, it’s still dirty," Toad said, taking it out.
He splashed the shirt in the tub again and again.
"I know! I’ll twist the shirt!" said Toad.
He twisted and hit the shirt against the tub.
Soap bubbles spilled over the side into a puddle.
"Ahhh!" Toad yelled, as he slipped and fell.
"Ow, my back hurts," cried Toad.
"And where’s the soap?"
He crawled around looking for the soap.
Toad was wet and covered in bubbles.
The possum burst into laughter.
"I’ve been watching!" she shouted.
"You've never washed anything in your life!
You are a big liar!"
"How dare you talk to me like that!" yelled Toad.
He stood up proudly in his wet dress.
"I am Toad! Rich and famous Toad!" he said.
"I will not be made fun of by a possum!"
The possum looked closely at Toad.
"Did you say you are a toad?" she asked.
She stepped closer.
"You are a toad!" she screamed.
Toad backed away from her.
"I don’t like toads at all!" she yelled.
She grabbed him by the leg.
"Stop! Let go of me!" cried Toad.
She swung him around three times!
"Ahhh," cried Toad. "I’m getting dizzy!"
"Get off my boat!" the possum yelled.
Then she let him go.
Toad flew through the air.
He went over the side of the boat.
"Ahhh!" screamed Toad. "I’m falling!"
With a splash, Toad fell into the water.
Toad coughed. "The water is cold!" he cried.
His bonnet was soaked.
A lily pad covered his head.
The possum looked back and laughed.
"I’ll get you!" yelled Toad, shaking his fist.
"You’ll be sorry!"
Toad swam to shore and climbed out.
"This dress is heavy, but I can still run!" said Toad.
He ran along the path beside the canal.
"Up I go!" yelled Toad as he jumped on the horse.
"Let me untie you, horse," cried Toad.
"Now you are as free as I am!"
"Stop! Stop!" yelled the possum.
"No one can stop Toad!" Toad shouted.
And he rode away laughing.
Toad raced the horse across the meadow.
Before long, the horse tired.
Toad didn’t mind slowing down.
"That awful possum is far behind," he said.
After a few miles, the horse stopped.
"Come on," said Toad, "keep going."
But the horse lowered its head to eat grass.
"I’m hungry too," thought Toad.
Toad got off the horse and walked.
Soon he came to a wide road.
"I don’t know which direction to go.
I hope someone comes by," he said.
Far down the road, Toad heard a noise.
It sounded like a faint vroom, vroom!
A cloud of dust came toward him.
"It’s a car!" yelled Toad.
Toad jumped up and down.
"Hooray!" he said.
"I’ll ask them for a ride.
Badger will be very surprised."
He stepped into the road and waved.
The car slowed down.
Suddenly Toad’s knees shook.
"Oh no!" cried Toad.
It was the car from The Red Lion!
"It’s the car I stole!" cried Toad.
"It’s all over! Back to prison for me!
I’ll be in chains!"
Toad fainted and fell in the road.
The car came near and stopped.
"Oh dear! How sad!" said the driver.
"It’s a poor old washwoman."
The driver and his two friends stared at Toad.
"She fainted in the heat!" said the raccoon.
"Maybe she didn’t eat today," said the squirrel.
The raccoon and squirrel got out of the car.
"Put her in the back with me," said the chipmunk.
The raccoon and squirrel gently lifted Toad.
They put him on a cushion in the backseat.
"They don’t know who I am!" thought Toad.
The raccoon started the car.
They drove down the road again.
"Look!" said the chipmunk.
"The breeze is doing her good."
"How are you feeling?" asked the raccoon.
"Much better," said Toad in a weak voice.
Toad watched him turn the steering wheel.
"I was only wondering . . . ," Toad said.
"Could I sit next to you?
It’s too windy back here now."
"Sure!" said the raccoon.
The chipmunk helped Toad into the front.
He sat between the driver and the squirrel.
"Please, sir," Toad asked the raccoon,
"would you let me drive?"
"You?" asked the raccoon.
He looked at his friends and laughed.
"I’ve been watching you," said Toad sweetly.
"It looks easy."
"Well . . . ," said the raccoon.
"Let her try," said the chipmunk.
"She won’t do any harm."
Toad smiled.
The raccoon stopped the car.
"Well, why not?" he said.
"I’ll let you drive for a while."
"Oh, thank you, sir!" said Toad.
Toad jumped into the driver’s seat.
"Now turn the key," said the raccoon.
"Vroom!" went the engine.
Toad pretended he didn’t know what to do.
"Put your foot on the gas pedal," said the raccoon.
"Now press it slowly."
The car started down the road.
"She did it!" said the chipmunk.
"Imagine!" said the squirrel.
"A washwoman is driving a car!"
Toad went a little faster.
Then he drove faster still.
"Be careful, washwoman!" yelled the squirrel.
The raccoon tried to take the wheel.
Toad pushed him away.
Toad sped up as fast as the car would go!
"I am no washwoman!" shouted Toad.
"I am Toad! I steal cars!
I break out of prison! I am fearless!"
The squirrel and the chipmunk screamed.
"Grab him!" cried the raccoon.
The chipmunk pulled at Toad’s bonnet.
"He stole our car!" shouted the squirrel.
The raccoon tried to grab the wheel.
"Get your hands off!" shouted Toad.
They fought over the wheel.
And the car sped crazily down the road.
Toad fought with the raccoon in the speeding car.
The car went side to side on the road.
"Give me the wheel!" cried the raccoon.
"Get your hands off me!" yelled Toad.
Toad grabbed the wheel with all his might.
The car turned suddenly.
"Ahhh!" cried Toad.
The car crashed through a row of bushes.
"Oh no!" cried the raccoon.
Then the car crashed into a muddy pond.
Toad bounced out of the car.
He landed in soft grass.
The driver and his friends landed in the mud .
"Look at you!" laughed Toad.
"Call the police!" they yelled.
"I have to escape!" cried Toad.
Toad hopped up and ran.
He climbed over fences.
He jumped across ditches.
He crawled through bushes.
Toad ran and ran until he was far away.
"Toad wins again!" he laughed.
He walked happily through a field.
He sang a little song.
"Who asked them to give him a ride?
Clever Toad!
Who tricked them to let him drive?
Clever Toad!
"Who made them muddy and mad?
Who made them sorry and sad?
Who escaped and feels so glad?
Clever Toad! Clever Toad!"
"I escaped again!" thought Toad.
He walked through a field singing his song.
"Who escaped and feels so glad?
Clever Toad! Clever Toad!"
"Oh, what a wonderful song," said Toad.
"It’s the best song I ever wrote!"
He sang it again as loud as he could.
Suddenly Toad stopped and listened.
He heard a noise behind him.
He turned around to look.
Two policemen were running his way.
"Oh no!" said Toad. "Poor me!"
The raccoon ran with the policemen.
"There he is!" the raccoon cried.
"We’ll get you!" yelled the police.
Suddenly afraid, Toad ran.
"I’m so stupid!" cried Toad.
"I was singing too loudly.
I was too pleased with myself!"
Toad looked back.
The police waved their clubs.
"We’ll take you to prison, Toad!" they shouted.
"I can’t let them catch me!" cried Toad.
Toad huffed and puffed as he ran.
"I’m a bit too fat to run so much!" Toad said.
Toad was getting tired.
But then he looked back.
The police were getting closer!
"Must go faster!" thought Toad, running wildly.
Suddenly the ground below was gone!
Toad flipped over in the air.
Splash! He landed in water.
Toad splashed his arms in the water.
The water was flowing fast.
He held his head above the waves.
"I’m in the river!" he cried.
The waves turned him over.
"Oh my!" Toad yelled. "Help!"
His head went under.
He swallowed a gulp of water.
Toad’s head popped up again.
He coughed.
"I’ll never steal another car!" cried Toad.
"I’ll never sing another song!"
Under the water he went again.
"Oh dear," he said with a splash.
His head popped up once more.
"I’ll never tell another lie!" he cried.
Toad grabbed the reeds on the bank.
But the reeds broke off in his hands.
In the riverbank ahead was a round hole.
"Maybe I can grab onto it," said Toad.
"Here it comes!" cried Toad.
The waves carried him closer.
Now the dark opening was just above him.
Toad reached for the edge of the hole.
"I made it!" said Toad, holding on.
He was only halfway out of the water.
"I’ll catch my breath here," he said.
Two bright eyes shone out of the hole.
"What’s that?" said Toad.
Then a small brown face appeared.
It was Rat!
Rat stuck out a brown paw.
He grabbed Toad by the neck.
"Here you go, Toad!" said Rat.
Rat pulled Toad into his hole.
"Oh Ratty!" cried Toad.
"My life has been awful!
Everyone was chasing me!
I’ve suffered so much!"
"Well, you’re safe now," said Rat.
Rat patted Toad’s head.
Then Toad smiled proudly.
"I escaped from jail!" he shouted.
"And I stole a horse!
Oh, I am a clever Toad!
I’ll tell you all about it!"
